```{r}
source("R/clt_helpers.R")
```

## 1. The population
```{r}
set.seed(student_id)
x <- rnorm(10000)

hist(x, breaks = 40, probability = TRUE,
     col = "skyblue", border = "white",
     main = "Population: Individual Standard Normal Values",
     xlab = "Individual value")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
data.frame(
  quantity  = c("Mean", "SD", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis"),
  theory    = c(0, 1, 0, 0),
  simulated = round(c(mean(x), sd(x), skew(x), kurt(x)), 3)
)
```
The standard normal population is symmetric and bell-shaped, centered at 0 with SD 1. About 68% of values fall within 1 of the mean and about 95% within 2. Its skewness and excess kurtosis are both 0, and the simulated values from 10,000 draws agree closely. This population never changes during the experiment. Only the distribution of the sample means changes as n grows.

## 2. Prediction
For a normal population, the sample mean is exactly normal for every n: Xbar ~ N(0, 1/sqrt(n)). I therefore predict that the sampling distribution passes all four criteria at every tested n, including n = 2. The population skewness and excess kurtosis are both 0, so the skewness and kurtosis of the means should be 0 up to simulation noise (about +/-0.011 and +/-0.022 with B = 50,000), well inside my cutoffs. This population also serves as a baseline check on my criteria: if a distribution that is exactly normal failed them, the criteria or my code would be at fault.

## 3. My criterion
I decided on these criteria before running any simulations (see the README).
A sampling distribution of the mean is "approximately normal" when ALL of
the following hold:

1. |skewness| < 0.2
2. |excess kurtosis| < 0.3
3. The normal Q-Q plot follows the line across the central region with no systematic curve. Small random departures at the extreme tails are acceptable.
4. The simulated SD of the sample means is within 2% of the theoretical   standard error, sigma / sqrt(n) (ratio between 0.98 and 1.02).

I report the smallest tested n at which this and every larger tested n pass all four criteria.

## 4. Simulation
I simulated B = 50,000 sample means at each of 12 sample sizes. I used the same grid and the same B as for the exponential so the populations can be compared directly. The grid includes n = 30 to test the common rule of thumb.

```{r}
ns  <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 300)
res <- run_clt(function(n) rnorm(n), ns, mu = 0, sigma = 1, B = 50000)
```

## 5. Evidence
### Numerical table
```{r}
tab <- add_checks(res$table)
knitr::kable(
  tab[, c("n", "skew", "excess_kurt", "sd_ratio",
          "skew_ok", "kurt_ok", "se_ok", "all_numeric")],
  digits = 3
)
```

```{r}
smallest_n(tab)
```
By the numeric criteria, the smallest tested n at which this and every larger tested n pass is 2, as predicted. Every row passes all three numeric criteria.

### Histograms with the normal curve
```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
for (n in c(2, 30, 300)) {
  plot_clt(res$means[[as.character(n)]], n, mu = 0, sigma = 1)
}
```
### Q-Q plots
- n = 2: The points follow the line through the middle, with only small random scatter at the extreme ends. This is my reference for what random wiggle looks like when the answer is exactly normal.
- n = 30: (describe what you see)
- n = 300: (describe what you see)

## 6. Comparison with theory

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  tab[, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd", "theory_se", "sd_ratio")],
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot(tab$n, tab$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "x",
     ylim = c(0.95, 1.05), xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)",
     ylab = "Simulated SD / theoretical SE",
     main = "Normal: standard error check")
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(0.98, 1.02), col = "gray50", lty = 2)
```
The simulated means are all very close to the theoretical mean of 0, and the simulated SD of the means agrees with 1 / sqrt(n) within about 0.4% at every sample size, including n = 2.

## 7. Conclusion
**Smallest tested n at which the sampling distribution is approximately normal (all four criteria): n = 2.**

All three numeric criteria pass at every tested n, and the Q-Q plots follow the line at every n I inspected. This is the expected result: the mean of normal observations is exactly normal for any n, so the CLT is not needed. n = 2 is the smallest value in my grid; n = 1 is trivially normal, since a single observation is just the population itself.

## 8. Surprises and limitations
- This population served as a baseline check on my criteria and code. An exactly normal distribution passed everything at every n, so a failure for another population reflects that population and not a bug or an overly strict cutoff.
- I used the Q-Q plots from this file as my reference for what random wiggle in the extreme tails looks like when the answer is exactly normal.
- With B = 50,000, skewness varies by about +/-0.011 and kurtosis by about +/-0.022 from run to run, so small nonzero values here are noise.
- Skewness, kurtosis, and the SD check cannot show a failure of normality that is smaller than that noise.
